claims.text: Available conventional analytical conductivity approaches for HfNbTaTiZr are based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional analytical approaches neglect significant effects from oxygen impurities.
Conventional analytical approaches neglect finite-temperature anharmonic effects.
Neglecting oxygen impurities and finite-temperature anharmonicity causes systematic errors in predicted conductivity.
The proposed method combines machine learning trained on temperature-dependent experimental data with first-principles simulations.
The first-principles component incorporates oxygen-induced lattice distortions and phonon interactions.
Oxygen produces defect states and local lattice distortions in bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen-induced defect states and local lattice distortions modify phonon scattering.
Oxygen-induced defect states and local lattice distortions modify electronic transport.
Extrinsic oxygen-related defect scattering dominates conductivity behavior from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Intrinsic phonon scattering dominates conductivity behavior from approximately 300 to 1200 K.
Training on experimental data containing defect effects enables the machine-learning component to tune first-principles predictions to the actual scattering landscape.
Explicit treatment of defects and finite-temperature lattice dynamics will improve conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr relative to perfect-crystal analytical approaches.
The integrated model will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy by roughly 20–30% over traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The model will reproduce defect-induced scattering behavior at low temperatures.
The model will reproduce phonon-scattering effects at high temperatures.
The model is primarily applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen concentrations around 1 wt.% in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Accuracy in the 200–300 K interval and at substantially different oxygen concentrations requires additional validation.
